q: Why are CHB walls reinforced both ways?
o: To resist earthquake and wind loads
n: Bars in both directions give CHB walls tensile capacity against earthquake and wind loads. Source: NSCP 2015, Chapter 7.

q: What is the standard spacing of horizontal reinforcement in CHB walls?
n: Horizontal reinforcement in CHB walls is placed every 0.60 m (every 3 courses). Source: Fajardo, Simplified Construction Estimate.

q: What is the minimum dead load requirement for a wall?
n: The item takes a nominal minimum wall dead load of 1 kPa. Actual wall dead loads come from the material weights in NSCP Table 204-1. Source: NSCP 2015, Chapter 2 (dead loads).

q: What may be built along side or rear property lines on fairly flat lots?
n: On fairly flat lots, firewalls and perimeter walls may be built along side or rear property lines, within NBC firewall limits. Source: NBC (PD 1096) IRR, Rule VII, Sec. 704.

q: What is the most commonly used size of reinforcing bars for both vertical and horizontal reinforcement in CHB walls (in millimeters)?
n: 10 mm bars are the most common for both vertical and horizontal CHB wall reinforcement. Source: Fajardo, Simplified Construction Estimate.

q: What is Figure A, a bolt used to fasten a structure to a foundation, typically for holding steel columns or beams in place?
n: Figure A is an anchor bolt, cast into the foundation to hold steel columns or beams through their base plates. Source: AISC Design Guide 1 (Base Plate and Anchor Rod Design); Ching.

q: What is Figure B, a metal plate used to connect and reinforce the joints of a truss, beam, or column in structural applications?
n: Figure B is a gusset plate, a steel plate that connects and reinforces joints of trusses, beams or bracing. Source: Ching, A Visual Dictionary of Architecture.

q: What is Figure C, a metal connector used to join wood trusses, often in the form of a metal plate with nails driven through it?
n: Figure C is a gang nail (truss plate), a toothed metal plate pressed into timber truss joints. Source: Ching, Building Construction Illustrated; TPI 1.

q: What is Figure D, a type of bolt that expands when tightened, used to anchor structures to concrete or masonry?
n: Figure D is an expansion bolt, which expands as it is tightened to anchor into concrete or masonry. Source: Ching, A Visual Dictionary of Architecture.

q: What is Figure E, a type of stud welded to steel beams or plates to improve the shear connection between concrete and steel in composite construction?
n: Figure E is a shear stud, welded to steel beams to give composite shear connection with the concrete slab. Source: NSCP 2015, Chapter 5 (composite members); AWS D1.1.

q: What is Item A?
n: Item A is a post base, which anchors a wood post to the footing and keeps it clear of moisture. Source: Simpson Strong-Tie connector catalogue; Ching.

q: What is Item B?
n: Item B is a truss (joist) hanger, which supports a truss or joist end from a carrying member. Source: Simpson Strong-Tie connector catalogue.

q: What is Item C?
n: Item C is a sleeve anchor, an expansion anchor with a sleeve for concrete or masonry. Source: Hilti/Simpson anchor catalogues.

q: Figure 16-B: What is Item D?
n: Item D is a post cap, connecting a beam to the top of a post. Source: Simpson Strong-Tie connector catalogue.

q: What is Item E used for?
n: Item E shows glass railing connectors (spider or standoff fittings), used for glass installations. Source: Manufacturer catalogues (e.g., CRL); Ching.

q: Which connector is used for drywall construction?
n: Figure B is a light-gauge framing angle used in drywall partitions. Source: Gypsum Association GA-216; Ching.

q: Which connector is used for steel construction?
n: Figure E is a rivet, used to connect steel members. Source: Ching, A Visual Dictionary of Architecture.

q: Which connector is used for roofing work?
n: Figure C is a roof anchor for fall-arrest protection, used in roofing work. Source: DOLE OSHS Rule 1414 (fall protection); manufacturer data.

q: Which connector is used for woodworking?
n: Figure A is a nail plate, used to join timber members in woodworking and trusses. Source: Ching, Building Construction Illustrated.

q: Which connector is used for both concrete and steel construction?
n: Figure D joins steel and concrete (shear studs or anchors), so it is used in both. Source: NSCP 2015, Chapter 5.

q: What short bar extends from one concrete element into another, such as from footing to column?
n: A dowel is a short bar extending from one concrete element into another, such as from footing to column, to transfer force. Source: NSCP 2015, Sec. 416.3 (footing-to-column transfer).

q: Howis a pre-stressed concrete element typically connected to reinforced concrete?
n: Precast or prestressed members are commonly connected to cast-in-place concrete with dowels grouted or cast into both. Source: PCI Design Handbook; NSCP 2015 Chapter 4.

q: What is the primary function of a shear stud?
o: To connect steel decking to beams
To distribute the load from the slab to the beam
n: Shear studs transfer horizontal shear so the slab and beam act compositely, distributing load between slab and beam. Source: NSCP 2015, Chapter 5 (composite members).

q: Which masonry anchor has a split malleable-iron cone that expands as it's tightened?
n: An expansion bolt (anchor) has a split malleable-iron shield or cone that expands in the hole as it is tightened. Source: Ching, A Visual Dictionary of Architecture.

q: Which element is placed at construction joints to ensure load transfer between two separate concrete pours?
n: Dowel bars at construction joints transfer load across the joint between separate pours. Source: ACI 224.3R; ACI 302.1R.

q: What is the surface where a concrete pour was stopped and later resumed?
n: A construction joint is the surface where a pour was stopped and later resumed. It is made where placement must stop. The old surface is roughened and cleaned so the new pour bonds to it. Source: ACI 224.3R.

q: What material is commonly used as a filler for an expansion joint?
n: Bituminous fibreboard or bitumen-impregnated filler is the classic expansion-joint filler. Source: ASTM D1751; ACI 224.3R.

q: What is a seismic gap for?
o: Keeping adjacent buildings from pounding in an earthquake
n: A seismic gap separates adjacent buildings so they do not pound against each other in an earthquake. Source: NSCP 2015, Sec. 208.7.2.11 (building separation).

q: Which joint absorbs thermal movement, vibration and settlement or seismic movement?
n: An expansion joint absorbs thermal movement, vibration, settlement and seismic movement between parts of a structure. Source: ACI 224.3R.

q: What long light-gauge members hold finishes such as drywall or ceiling boards?
n: Metal furring (light-gauge channels) holds finishes such as drywall or ceiling boards. Source: Ching, Building Construction Illustrated; ASTM C754.

q: Which steel plate connects truss members?
n: A gusset plate connects truss members at a joint. Source: Ching, A Visual Dictionary of Architecture.

q: What diagonal light members join parts into a built-up strut?
n: Lacing, light diagonal bars, joins the parts of a built-up strut or column so they act as one. Source: AISC 360; NSCP 2015 Chapter 5.

q: What is the minimum splice length for reinforcing bars (rebar)?
n: A lap of about 40 bar diameters (40db) is a common rule of thumb for tension splices. Code values depend on bar size, f'c and fy (Class B = 1.3 ld). Source: NSCP 2015, Sec. 425.5; common detailing practice.

q: What does a gusset plate do in a steel truss?
o: Anchors the truss to the foundation
n: In a steel truss, gusset plates join the members at a joint and transfer forces between them. Source: Ching, A Visual Dictionary of Architecture.
